title: What an operating system actually does
objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain, without jargon, the four jobs every operating system does — and why each one matters to security.

blocks.text: You have used an operating system every day for years. You have probably never had to say what one is. That is fine for using a computer and useless for defending one, because almost every security control you will ever configure is really an operating system feature with a product name on top.
Here is the whole idea in one sentence: an operating system is the program that decides which other programs get to use the hardware, and on what terms.
Everything an OS does falls into four buckets. Once these four are clear, most of Linux follows from them.

blocks.alt: Programs such as a browser, an editor, a shell command and a background service all sit above the operating system. The operating system does four jobs — runs things by sharing the CPU, hands out memory, stores files, and decides who may do what. Below it sit the CPU, memory, disk and network card, none of which programs touch directly.
blocks.caption: Nothing you run reaches the hardware on its own. That is the whole idea.

rows: Decide which program uses the CPU, and when
Give each program its own memory and keep them apart
Why one crashed program does not take the machine down
Turn a disk into files and folders with names

blocks.text: The kernel is the part that enforces

The core of the operating system is called the kernel. It is the only code that talks to the hardware directly. Your programs do not get to touch the disk or the network card themselves — they ask the kernel, and the kernel decides whether to do it.

That asking has a name: a system call. When a text editor saves a file, it makes a system call that means roughly "please write these bytes to this file". The kernel checks whether this user is allowed to write that file, and either does it or refuses.

blocks.title: Why this is the whole security story in miniature
blocks.text: Every permission check, every audit log, every "access denied" starts here. If an attacker can get their code to run inside the kernel, there is nothing left above it to say no. That is why kernel patches are urgent in a way that most updates are not.
Two worlds: kernel space and user space

You will see the terms kernel space and user space constantly. Kernel space is where the kernel runs, with full access to the hardware. User space is where everything else runs — your browser, your editor, the web server — each one boxed in, able to ask for things but not to take them.

items: A program crashing in user space kills that program
A failure in kernel space can take down the whole machine
Privilege escalation means getting more authority than you were given — most often an ordinary user gaining root's authority, while still running in user space

blocks.title: A mental model that will keep paying off
blocks.text: Think of the kernel as the only person with keys to the building, and every program as a visitor at the front desk. Visitors can request anything. The desk decides. Most security work comes down to what the kernel agrees to do, and which user is asking.

cheatsheet: An OS decides which programs use the hardware, and on what terms
Four jobs: run programs, manage memory, store files, decide who may do what
The kernel is the only code that touches hardware directly
Programs ask the kernel for things using system calls
User space = boxed-in programs · kernel space = full access
Privilege escalation = getting more authority than you were given — most often from an ordinary user account to root

videoCueQuestions.prompt: A program wants to write a file to disk. What actually happens?

choices.A: The program writes to the disk hardware directly
choices.B: The program asks the kernel, which checks permission and then writes
choices.C: The program asks the antivirus for permission first
choices.D: The disk decides whether to accept the write

videoCueQuestions.explanation: Programs in user space never touch hardware directly. They make a system call, and the kernel decides whether to carry it out. That decision point is where permissions are enforced.

videoCueQuestions.prompt: Why does one program crashing usually not take down the whole machine?

choices.B: Because the OS restarts crashed programs automatically
choices.C: Because each program runs in user space with its own memory, isolated from the others
choices.D: Because crashes only affect the window that is on screen

videoCueQuestions.explanation: Memory management keeps programs apart. A crash in user space is contained to that program. A failure inside the kernel is a different matter — that can take the machine with it.

videoCueQuestions.prompt: Which of these is the operating system's job, not an add-on security product's job?

choices.A: Deciding whether this user may open this file
choices.B: Showing a dashboard of last month's alerts
choices.C: Emailing a report to the security team

videoCueQuestions.explanation: Access decisions are a core OS function. Security products mostly observe, report on, and add policy around decisions the operating system is already making.

checkpoint.prompt: In one line: what is an operating system?

choices.A: The set of applications installed on a machine
choices.B: The firmware built into the motherboard
choices.C: The referee deciding which programs get hardware
choices.D: The window manager and desktop you see on screen

checkpoint.explanation: The desktop is one visible part, and firmware sits below the OS. The defining job is arbitrating access to hardware on behalf of programs.

checkpoint.prompt: Which of these are jobs of the operating system? (Select all that apply.)

choices.A: Scheduling which program gets the CPU
choices.B: Keeping each program's memory separate from the others
choices.C: Turning a disk into named files and folders
choices.D: Enforcing which user may read which file
choices.E: Writing the business logic that belongs to the application

checkpoint.explanation: The first four are the OS's four jobs. Business logic belongs to the application — the OS only decides whether that application is allowed to do what it asks.

checkpoint.prompt: Why do kernel vulnerabilities get treated more urgently than most application bugs?

choices.A: The kernel enforces every access decision
choices.B: Kernel bugs are always easier to exploit
choices.C: Application bugs cannot lead to any data loss
choices.D: Kernels are written in older languages

checkpoint.explanation: Code running there has nothing above it saying no. It is about position, not difficulty. Controls above the kernel depend on the kernel being trustworthy; once that assumption breaks, the controls built on it stop meaning anything.
